entries.title: CAR: Scores killed in landslide at illegal gold mine
entries.summary: More than 100 workers may have been killed in a landslide at an illegal mine near the Central African Republic's border with Cameroon, say authorities. More miners are trapped and hope for their survival is fading.
entries.content:
Africa

CAR: Scores killed in landslide at illegal gold mine

August 19, 2026

More than 100 workers may have been killed in a landslide at an illegal mine near the Central African Republic's border with Cameroon, say authorities. More miners are trapped and hope for their survival is fading.

Authorities in the western part of the Central African Republic (CAR) say dozens of laborers were killed Tuesday afternoon when a landslide buried them at the illegal Zamboye mining site near the Cameroon border — about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the town of Baboua.

Death tolls have ranged from "at least 30" initially to "over 100," with local authorities saying the window for survival is quickly closing for the many miners still buried at the site.

Video uploaded to social media platforms showed bodies churning in earth as the landslide lunges into the open-pit site beneath, burying everything in its path.

Frantic rescue activities continued on Wednesday with reports of mud-covered young men and women pulling bodies from the mine's collapsed entrance, as still more screamed for help.

"The collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating," was given as the cause of the collapse by the Baboua public prosecutor's office, which also announced that an investigation had been launched.

CAR government spokesman Evariste Ngamana expressed sympathy and pledged the government was "working hard to provide relief and assistance."

What is the state of CAR's 'artisanal' mines?

Improvised "artisanal" mines in the gold-rich region are often illegal and shoddily built, following limited or no safety standards whatsoever.

That means the thousands of laborers who use their hands to mine for gold every day, put their lives at risk each time they enter one.

Serious accidents are a regular occurrence and these are usually very deadly.

Dozens of miners have been killed in landslides in the area since the beginning of the year.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Germany condemns Israeli minister's call to 'remove' Palestinians
entries.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has denounced a call by Israel's far-right security minister to carry out "targeted killings" of Palestinians in Gaza. The outrage spans the entire political spectrum.
entries.content:
Germany

German lawmakers condemn Israeli minister's Gaza remarks

August 19, 2026

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has denounced a call by Israel's far-right security minister to carry out "targeted killings" of Palestinians in Gaza. The outrage spans the entire political spectrum.

"I think that targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza," said Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel's national security minister, on Monday, sparking worldwide outrage.

The hard-liner in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Cabinet also described exactly what he had in mind: Every night, 30 or 40 Palestinians should be "removed." Ben-Gvir emphasized that he was not only referring to militant Palestinians who posed an immediate threat, adding that there are people in the Gaza Strip who do not deserve to live.

On Wednesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz denounced the statement made by the controversial Israeli politician. "The chancellor strongly condemns Minister Ben-Gvir's inhumane statements, which violate international law — they are unacceptable," said a government spokesperson in Berlin. Merz is officially on vacation.

The spokesperson also criticized Israel's plans to further accelerate settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Merz is following the latest developments "with great concern."

The spokesperson said there must be no further steps toward annexation, adding: "As the occupying power, Israel must treat Palestinians with dignity, protect their property and ensure public administration and humanitarian aid."

Vice Chancellor Klingbeil: 'A line has truly been crossed'

Merz's deputy from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, had already called for consequences on Tuesday.

"These are statements that we, as the federal government, cannot accept in any way," he told the private TV station Sat1. Klingbeil said that sanctions are being discussed at the European level, adding: "This must now be looked at very seriously." Despite all its solidarity with the state of Israel, Germany must not remain silent, he stressed. A line has now "truly been crossed."

Hildegard Bentele, a German member of the European Parliament from the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also supports sanctions against Ben-Gvir, telling DW on Tuesday that she had been calling for them for a year.

"Eliminating individuals is unacceptable to us in Europe," she emphasized.

Many countries have imposed entry bans on Ben-Gvir

Several countries have already imposed entry bans on Ben-Gvir, including Australia, France, the United Kingdom, Canada, New Zealand, Norway and the Netherlands.

Jürgen Hardt, the foreign policy spokesperson for the conservative parliamentary group in Germany's lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, also supports the call for European Union sanctions against Ben-Gvir. 

"The EU should sanction him as a statement on the universal validity of human dignity and human rights," Hardt told the news magazine Politico. Hardt said he is convinced that an Israeli Cabinet without Ben-Gvir would bring Europe and Israel closer together again.

Calls for sanctions and a halt to arms exports to Israel

The environmentalist Green Party, an opposition party in the German parliament, has also demanded harsh consequences.

"I urge the federal government to impose an entry ban on this man and to advocate for similar sanctions to be imposed at the European level as well," Green Party leader Franziska Brantner told Politico.

This is not the first time Ben-Gvir has drawn attention for his appalling calls for violence against Palestinians, Brantner emphasized. She also called for Germany to follow the example of other countries and impose sanctions: "It's time for Germany to join these nations."

Lea Reisner, a politician from the socialist Left Party, went further on Deutschlandfunk public radio, calling for a halt to all German arms exports to Israel.

Josef Schuster: Ben-Gvir's comments 'deeply shameful and irresponsible'

Germany's Central Council of Jews in Germany also reacted with horror to Ben-Gvir's call for mass killings of Palestinians. The president of the Central Council, Josef Schuster, told the Catholic News Agency that Ben-Gvir's statements were diametrically opposed to Jewish values and damage Israel's reputation.

"Itamar Ben-Gvir's behavior is deeply shameful and irresponsible," said Schuster, adding that it illustrates the danger posed by far-right forces.

Kirsten Fehrs, chair of the Council of the Protestant Church in Germany, described Ben-Gvir's statements on the social media platform Threads as an "attack on humanity." The bishop stressed that there must be a shared conviction across religions that every human being possesses inalienable dignity because they are made in God's image.

"No one can bestow this dignity, and no one can take it away," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: India 'Cockroach' movement takes aim at government schools
entries.summary: The student protest movement is turning its grassroots network into a nationwide campaign to audit neglected government schools and pressure authorities to act.
entries.content:
India

India 'Cockroach' movement takes aim at government schools

August 19, 2026

The student protest movement is turning its grassroots network into a nationwide campaign to audit neglected government schools and pressure authorities to act.

The student protest movement in India known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) scored a major victory in July after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan stepped down following weeks of demonstrations in Delhi.

Now, the movement is aiming its campaign for accountability at improving India's government schools.

Last week on India's Independence Day, the CJP launched a nationwide campaign asking citizens to inspect government schools, document what is missing and pressure local authorities to fix basic facilities.

Dubbed "Fix the Schools," the campaign aims to mobilize citizens to identify problems locally and make them public.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke launched a campaign in the Indian state of Maharashtra from his native village in Hingoli district. He spoke with students and documented what he said were broken windows, lack of clean drinking water, missing classroom benches and unusable bathrooms.

"No matter which political party ruled, nobody worked for government schools in states. Now there is a need, and we can make them work by asking questions," said Dipke.

Government officials did not respond to DW's requests for comment on the CJP's accusations.

What does the plan call for?

The CJP has prepared assessment forms that parents, students and residents can use to document issues with local government schools. They are being asked to record video evidence, complete the assessment and send the material to CJP.

The organization plans to compile the reports into a public record of neglected schools and use them to pressure local authorities to respond.

The CJP has said the campaign will focus on five basic requirements: functioning toilets, electricity, clean drinking water, classroom benches and the quality of midday meals.

One element is to publicly recognize village heads who improve their local schools. The CJP plans to use before-and-after evidence to highlight villages where conditions have improved.

The organization has set an initial target of auditing at least 100 rural government schools over the next two months and pressing authorities to act on the findings.

CJP seeks to expand support

The youth-led CJP began in May as a campaign calling for accountability over a scandal involving a highly competitive university entrance exam. The news that the question sheet had been leaked ahead of the exam date in early May exposed long-running grievances over privileged access for some students.

Fueled by millions of young followers on social media, the movement soon tapped into wider frustrations over unemployment, shrinking opportunities and an education system many young Indians believe has failed them.

After the education minister stepped down, and the government promised steps toward accountability for those involved in the exam paper leaks, the CJP has shifted focus.

However, to be effective in localities around India, the youth-based movement, which has initially mainly been based in Delhi, will need to broaden its appeal.

This comes as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in his Independence Day address, placed youth power at the center of his vision for a developed India.

India's youth a political force

Aruna Roy, a prominent Indian social activist and former civil servant who helped lead a grassroots movement that resulted in India's landmark Right to Information Act in 2005, said the CJP's campaign could tap into a wider constituency of young people seeking greater accountability.

"The demands at Jantar Mantar resonated with young people across the country," Roy said, referring to the location in central Delhi where the protests were based.

"It was, in many cases, a spontaneous revolt against the state for failing to deliver on promises affecting their education, employment and future," Roy told DW.

"When young people have decided to fight against the destruction of their dreams, they are formidable," she added.

CJP opens door for 'citizen audits'

Responsibility for government school infrastructure is spread across state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies, while conditions vary widely across India.

The CJP's new campaign is a test of whether the movement's ability to mobilize students, volunteers, money and public attention outside traditional political structures can be sustained beyond last month's high-profile victory.

Amrita Johri, an activist and transparency advocate, said CJP had tapped into larger issues with India's education system.

"Millions of young people have lost precious years and resources because of repeated failures to ensure fair examinations, with little accountability for those responsible," Johri told DW.

"Every government school should publicly disclose its spending, infrastructure, teacher vacancies and midday meal provision," Johri said.

"The CJP can make this meaningful by training volunteers to systematically document problems and follow up, while helping local communities use tools such as the Right to Information to demand change," she added.

Social activist Roy said citizen audits could turn public anger into sustained pressure for accountability.

"Citizen audits are vital because they expose corruption and the arbitrary use of power and bring people into the struggle for accountability," she said.

The campaign gives parents and residents a direct role in documenting what they see around them. CJP has said they do not need to wait for an official inspection to identify a broken toilet, a school without drinking water or classrooms without basic furniture.

What comes next?

The first test will be whether its target of 100 schools produces visible changes, and whether the model can be replicated beyond the places where CJP already has organizers and supporters.

The organization has also indicated that it could extend the citizen audit model to public healthcare facilities, widening its focus from education to other basic government services.

N. Sai Balaji, former president of the All India Students' Association, said CJP was broadening the fight over education reform and creating the possibility of convergence with student movements already campaigning on higher education.

"The two will meet, and there is a clear synergy. The impact will be felt as the momentum builds," Balaji told DW.

For a movement that began with a protest over examination irregularities, the next phase is less about taking to the streets and more about documenting what citizens encounter in their everyday lives.

"We have built a new parliament, a new PM house. Why have we not been able to build new schools in our villages? Do we not consider the children of farmers and laborers the future of our country?" asked CJP leader Dipke in a video message.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Why the US is going after the International Criminal Court
entries.summary: Marco Rubio, Donald Trump's secretary of state, has announced sanctions against two members of the International Criminal Court, including its president. Rubio's pressure on the court has far-reaching consequences.
entries.content:
United States of America

Why the US is going after the International Criminal Court

August 19, 2026

Marco Rubio, Donald Trump's secretary of state, has announced sanctions against two members of the International Criminal Court, including its president. Rubio's pressure on the court has far-reaching consequences.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took aim at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Tuesday, calling it "corrupt and fatally politicized" and claiming it has "maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate."

He announced sanctions against the ICC president, Tomoko Akane of Japan, and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal. The sanctions include freezing of their US-held bank assets and largely cutting them off from the US financial system.

The ICC has been holding individuals accountable for war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity since 2002. The court is based in The Hague, just like the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is part of the United Nations and settles disputes between states.

Unlike the ICJ, the ICC has 125 members, not all 193 UN member states. The US, Russia and China are among the countries that have not joined, along with several states in Asia and North Africa.

Rubio had recently threatened to dismantle the court "brick by brick." In a statement in July, the State Department outlined a number of measures Washington is considering as part of its campaign against the court. These include visa restrictions on ICC staff and tougher sanctions targeting the court and affiliated organizations. It also suggested increased scrutiny of countries "that refuse to reject the ICC's illegitimate authority" while continuing to receive US assistance.

The US has clashed with the ICC before. But legal experts around the world say Washington's latest escalation marks a significant shift.

How Washington is piling pressure onto The Hague

"What the US and Marco Rubio have now essentially done is make public something that has been going on for more than a year," Andreas Schüller, co-director of the International Crimes and Legal Accountability Program at the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR) in Berlin, told DW in July.

"The US has been using various forms of diplomatic pressure against other countries in an effort to change their positions, and in some cases their voting behavior, toward the ICC," he added.

"The fact that it is now being declared a campaign shows that it is being pursued strategically, that it is broader in scope, and that other countries — including those that are not ICC members — are also being brought on board to help apply pressure."

A court to ensure no perpetrator can escape justice

The US is not a member of the International Criminal Court, meaning crimes committed on US soil do not fall under its jurisdiction. But the ICC can prosecute alleged atrocities committed in member states — a principle that led, for example, to arrest warrants being issued for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The ICC has its roots in the lessons of history. The Nuremberg trials after World War II, which put leading Nazi figures on trial, marked the birth of modern international criminal law. After war crimes tribunals were set up in the 1990s following the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia and the genocide in Rwanda, calls for a permanent court gained momentum.

For Kai Ambos, an international law expert at the University of Göttingen, the issue comes down to "the fundamental question of accountability" — whether in Ukraine, Iran or Gaza.

"It cannot be that such serious crimes are committed, regardless of the conflict, and those primarily responsible — above all government leaders and other figures in power — go unpunished. Nothing happens. That is unacceptable for victims, but ultimately for all of us," Ambos told DW before the recent US sanctions.

Should US citizens be in the dock?

In a short video address in July, Rubio said the court posed a threat to the entire US legal system.

"Border Patrol agents removing violent criminals from our country. American Marines risking their lives to defend our nation. … If we do nothing, they would all be left at the mercy of foreign judges thousands of miles away," he said.

No case against US citizens is currently pending before the ICC. The actions of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers take place largely on US territory, where the court has no jurisdiction.

The situation is different when it comes to the targeted killings of alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean: Former ICC prosecutor Luis Moreno Ocampo described them in November as potential crimes against humanity.

How can the court withstand the pressure?

Ambos fears that the so-called "chilling effect" could intensify — meaning, for example, that ICC prosecutors might become more cautious when dealing with US suspects. "And then there is the problem of overcompliance with sanctions — meaning that companies outside the US may also say: We will no longer work with the institution because it could put our business in the US at risk."

In 2025, the US State Department had already imposed a series of sanctions on the ICC and individual judges. The court responded by reducing its reliance on the US, replacing, for example, Microsoft Office software with a German open-source alternative.

ECCHR expert Schüller sees many small ways for member states to support the court. "If medium-sized powers and smaller states join forces against the US and come together as a pillar of support for international institutions, pushing back against this pressure, then that is the most important thing," he said.

The EU backed the ICC immediately after Rubio's previous threats in July. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul also defended the court, saying it makes the world "safer and more just."

Ironically, the US Senate held a similar view in 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In a resolution, it described the ICC as "an international tribunal that seeks to uphold the rule of law" and welcomed its investigations into Russia. One of the co-sponsors of the resolution, introduced by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, was none other than current US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

This article was originally written in German. This version was originally published on July 17, 2026, and updated on August 19, 2026, to reflect the recent US sanctions.

entries.title: Germany's rusting sea munitions are a toxic time bomb
entries.summary: Toxic chemicals from decades-old bombs are contaminating marine life in German waters. Scientists warn that the window to remove the weapons is closing.
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Toxic chemicals from decades-old bombs are contaminating marine life in German waters. Scientists warn that the window to remove the weapons is closing.

Beneath the seas off Germany's northern coast, vast quantities of bombs and other weapons are slowly rusting away.

They are part of an estimated 1.6 million metric tons of conventional munitions in the North Sea and Baltic Sea, a legacy of two world wars and the mass disposal of weapons after 1945.

How old weapons pose a new threat

For decades, the material was largely left alone unless it posed an explosive danger. But as metal casings corrode, a different problem is emerging.

Some weapons are remnants of fighting: mines, unexploded bombs and ammunition lost at sea. But huge quantities were deliberately dumped after Nazi Germany surrendered in 1945, as the Allies disposed of the country's vast arsenal.

What was once regarded as an explosive hazard has now become an environmental one.

"It's clear that due to corrosion of these items, compounds enter the marine ecosystem and enter marine life," Kiel University toxicologist Edmund Maser told DW. "It turned out that these compounds are toxic and carcinogenic, both for human life and also for marine life," he said.

Among the most toxic compounds in the old weapons is trinitrotoluene, or TNT, a military explosive. Jörn Scharsack of Germany's Thünen Institute of Fisheries Ecology looked for evidence of it in dab fish.

"We find TNT in the fish, or let's say, metabolization, degradation products of TNT," he said.

The quantities are tiny — measured in nanograms — and not every fish contains detectable levels. But researchers repeatedly find the compounds around old munitions hotspots. "It's low. But it's there."

How toxic munitions are affecting marine life

So far, the contamination does not appear to be making fish acutely sick.

"The fish look healthy when we take them out. They do not have more diseases in terms of viral, bacterial, parasite diseases," Scharsack told DW. There is, however, one recurring abnormal finding.

"What we see is tumors, so tumors in the liver. That pops up again and again."

Maser's group has also found munitions compounds in fish, as well as mussels.

Together with the Alfred Wegener Institute (AWI) in Bremerhaven, his team found liver abnormalities in more than 50% of fish living around some munitions dumping grounds and wrecks, compared with normal rates of just 1–2%.

Mussels, meanwhile, showed biochemical signs of oxidative stress. As TNT is metabolized, highly reactive forms of oxygen can damage proteins, lipids and even DNA. "This can be a step towards cancer," said Maser.

And the contamination does not stop with fish and mussels.

Maser's team has also detected TNT-related compounds in tissue samples from two stranded whales, showing that the chemicals are reaching animals at the top of the marine food web.

"That means that these compounds have arrived in top predators," he said.

Are Germany's sea munitions dangerous to humans?

That raises the obvious question: If TNT-related compounds are reaching top predators, are people who eat seafood at risk?

For now, both scientists say the answer is no.

Whales face more constant exposure through prey and surrounding water, while humans are exposed only occasionally through seafood.

"One would need to eat lots of fish to really reach a level where it's getting dangerous," said Scharsack. "I'm still going swimming. I'm still eating fish."

The concern is what happens as the munitions continue to deteriorate.

"I would say it's likely to get worse if we look at the ongoing corrosion of the munitions," Scharsack said.

"The shells are corroding. More and more of the toxic substances are lying open, exposed to the water."

The problem appears worse in the Baltic than the North Sea because weaker currents and water exchange allow leaking pollutants to linger rather than disperse.

What mussels reveal about TNT contamination

Maser's research suggests this may already be happening. His team examined archived mussels dating back to 1985 and found TNT-related contamination increasing steadily from around 2000 through 2022.

"It's low, but it's increasing," he said. "And we expect that over the coming decades, maybe two or three or four decades, we will have concentrations that could maybe harm the human seafood consumer."

Marine life is already under pressure from what Maser described as a "whole cocktail" of human-made pollutants, including microplastics, pesticides and pharmaceutical compounds. Munitions add another contaminant to that mix.

Unlike many of those pollutants, which are already dispersed through the oceans, bombs and mines remain physical objects that can be salvaged and disposed of.

And the window will not stay open forever.

Germany has long removed munitions posing an immediate danger, but only recently began pilot projects for systematic clearance to prevent environmental harm.

"The topic has been ignored for decades. Nobody wanted to talk about it," Scharsack said.

What are the challenges in clearing munitions?

In a study published in July, GEOMAR researcher Torsten Frey and colleagues identified 484 known or potential munitions piles in two areas of the Baltic Sea. But of the estimated 1.6 million tons of munitions in German waters, around 1.5 million tons have yet to be mapped, Frey told DW.

Recovering the munitions from known locations is no longer the main obstacle, Frey said, with specialist companies able to clear large quantities relatively quickly. "The bottleneck is the disposal and destruction of the recovered munitions."

Germany is developing an offshore treatment platform to help increase disposal capacity. "This will be a marathon, not a sprint," said Frey.

Even clearance will leave small pieces of explosive behind, some no larger than "a sugar cube." Maser is investigating whether marine bacteria and fungi could eventually break down these residues into CO2 and water.

The work is still at the laboratory stage and Maser stresses that it cannot replace physical clearance.

"We need more of these platforms," he said. "We need to start as early as possible."

"If we wait maybe 40 years, then maybe all these metal cases are corroded and we have then no chance to get these munition compounds out of the water," said Maser. "This is why we should act now."



Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

entries.title: Amid extreme heat, water grows scarce around Berlin
entries.summary: Though the German state of Brandenburg that wraps around Berlin is getting drier, it is also home to thirsty industrial plants such as Tesla and Red Bull. Is there enough water to go around?
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Though the German state of Brandenburg that wraps around Berlin is getting drier, it is also home to thirsty industrial plants such as Tesla and Red Bull. Is there enough water to go around?

For years, Petra Liesenfeld has witnessed falling groundwater levels in her hometown of Baruth. She has to water her garden far more often than she used to, and has seen some local trees completely dry out. At the same time, two beverage companies are looking to expand production in the area.

Mineral water has been bottled in the small town of Baruth, which lies around 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin, since the 1990s. The site is now run by Red Bull and Austrian beverage producer Rauch, who are planning a new canning factory and additional facilities. All in the middle of a water protection area.

The Baruth waterworks are licensed to extract a fixed amount of groundwater each year, just 8% of which goes to supply the town's roughly 4,300 residents with drinking water. The remaining 92% is reserved for Red Bull and Rauch, and is enough to cover the drinking water needs of 57,000 people. But exactly how much water the companies currently use is not made public.

This is legal under the existing contracts, said Peter Ilk, who until recently was the town's mayor and is considered a driving force behind the region's industrialization. He sees no problem with the way water is managed.

"We have always given priority to supplying the population. That is also written into all the contracts," he said, adding that it stands to reason that the companies need more than the town's residents. "That's how you end up with this ratio of around one to 10 in terms of consumption."

Old data informing current decisions

Hydrogeologist Irina Engelhardt from the Technical University in Berlin takes a more critical view, pointing out that the contracts, which are around 30 years old, are based on outdated information. Since then, groundwater levels, groundwater recharge and the way land is used have all changed significantly.

"I am concerned at how the water situation is developing in the state of Brandenburg," she said. "The volume that is actually available is currently being overestimated by the Brandenburg authorities."

Together with a citizens' initiative made up of local residents, she is calling for new, independent assessments — and for clear and open communication. Though the authorities granted them access to some groundwater monitoring documents, large parts were redacted, which some residents believe is a move to conceal information about changes in levels.

"We ask ourselves why there can't be more transparency if everything is aboveboard. Why isn't the public allowed to know?" said Petra Liesenfeld.

Exactly how much Red Bull and Rauch pay for their daily extraction of up to 7 million liters of groundwater is not public information.



DW approached both companies for comment, but by the time of publication, neither had responded.



For drought researcher Andreas Marx, this lack of transparency is problematic.

"By law, water is a public commodity. It cannot be privately owned. So, in my view, every decision made and every contract signed over its use should be open to the public," he said.

How dry is Brandenburg?

Germany — and Brandenburg — are still water-rich regions. Marx, who heads the Drought Monitor at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research, said "the challenge isn't adapting to permanent water scarcity but learning how to cope with dry periods that can last two or even three years."

Nevertheless, the water balance in the state, as elsewhere in Germany, is definitely changing. Since the 2018 drought, groundwater has not been sufficiently replenished in many places and higher temperatures and increasing evaporation are making it harder for reserves in deeper soil layers to recover.

This could cause even more problems in the future, as 95% of Brandenburg's drinking water comes from groundwater.

How much water does the energy transition need?

In Grünheide, in the eastern part of the state of Brandenburg, Tesla's Gigafactory has a permit to extract up to 1.4 million cubic meters of water per year and is planning to expand production to as many as 7,500 vehicles per week. Meanwhile, in recent years, residents have repeatedly been urged to save water.

"Many projects, including new schools and kindergartens, were put on hold because there simply wasn't enough water," said local resident Manu Hoyer.

Marx said when water resources are scarce, residents are generally the first to face restrictions because they're the easiest to limit. "Industrial companies are rarely restricted, because the economic consequences are much harder to assess," he said.

Copper for the energy transition — a risk to groundwater?

The potential for an additional water problem is brewing further south in Spremberg, where a large mine is planned. Over the coming decades, copper — which is essential for power grids, electric vehicles and the transition to clean energy — is set to be extracted from depths of up to 1,200 meters (about 4,000 feet).

Geotechnical engineer Michael Pfeifer said mine water from such depths is highly saline and sulfurous and requires extensive treatment.

"But the treatment plant proposed so far is nowhere near capable of doing what's actually required to clean the water to a standard where it could be safely discharged into the Spree," Pfeiffer said of the river that flows north toward Berlin.



The river water is already affected by decades of lignite mining in the region, and it is facing additional pressures. With lignite extraction set to end by 2038, the groundwater currently pumped into the Spree from the mines will no longer be available. As a result, dry summers could see the river carrying up to 75% less water, with far-reaching consequences for water resources all the way to Berlin.

Could rainfall be stored for future use?

One possible solution to the water problems facing the state around the German capital is artificial groundwater recharge, where excess water from periods of high rainfall is stored underground and used later.

Hydrogeologist Engelhardt is researching where this could be possible in the region.

"There are areas in Brandenburg — such as where Tesla is now located — where artificial groundwater recharge could meet almost the entire demand of the local drinking water supplier," she said.

However, enough available water is necessary for this solution to work.

For drought researcher Marx, one question remains crucial: What rules should determine how water is distributed between the population, agriculture, nature and industry during prolonged dry periods?

As the global temperature continues to rise, it's not just an issue reserved for Brandenburg — or even Germany.

This article was originally written in German.

Correction, August 19, 2026: An earlier version of this article misspelled the name of geotechnical engineer Michael Pfeifer. DW apologizes for the error.

entries.title: Israeli military to open criminal probes into 2 Gaza attacks
entries.summary: The investigations will focus on the killings of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind ⁠Rajab and 15 emergency aid workers in Gaza. The decision came after a review of 150 incidents concerning the conduct of Israeli troops.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

Israeli military to open criminal probes into 2 Gaza attacks

August 19, 2026

The investigations will focus on the killings of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind ⁠Rajab and 15 emergency aid workers in Gaza. The decision came after a review of 150 incidents concerning the conduct of Israeli troops.

The Israeli military has announced it will open criminal investigations into two high-profile attacks on Palestinians during the Gaza war.

In a report published Wednesday, the Israeli military said it had reviewed 150 incidents involving its troops in the Palestinian enclave and had made decisions about five of the cases.

The killings of 5-year-old Hind Rajab in 2024 and 15 Palestinian paramedics in 2025 would be subject to a criminal probe, the military said.

However, it said it would not take that step in the case of three other attacks in which aid workers from the charities World Central Kitchen and Doctors Without Borders (MSF) were killed.

The killing of Hind Rajab and 8 others in Gaza City

On January 29, 2024, Israeli forces fired on a car approaching them that was carrying a 5-year-old Palestinian girl, Hind Rajab, and her relatives in Gaza City, the military said in its report.

Five of the passengers were killed, while Rajab and her 15-year-old cousin Layan Hamada survived. Layan called the Palestinian Red Crescent, telling them a tank was approaching and her family members had been killed. According to a Red Crescent recording of the call, gunshots were heard, and Layan went silent. Rajab then stayed on the phone with the Red Crescent for hours, trapped in the car, as they tried to get permission from the military to rescue her, but contact was lost.

An ambulance dispatched to the site was also allegedly hit by a shell as it arrived.

Twelve days later, the bodies of Hind and seven of her relatives were recovered from the scene, along with two paramedics. The case drew international outrage.

"Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident," the Israeli military said in its report.

15 paramedics killed in Tel al-Sultan

On March 23, 2025, 15 emergency workers from the Red Crescent, Palestinian Civil Defense and the UN were killed when Israeli troops fired on their vehicles in Tel al-Sultan in northern Rafah.

Troops shot at a first ambulance that was driving to reach casualties, and then fired on other emergency vehicles that followed, according to phone footage and an account from the sole survivor.

The Israeli military said in its report that its troops were staging an early morning ambush against Hamas militants along a central access route and had fired at what they believed to be a Hamas vehicle. They then opened fire on other vehicles that arrived at the scene.

The troops then "decided to crush the vehicles and to cover the bodies with metal mesh," the military report said.

UN officials said that 15 bodies were recovered from a grave in the sand near vehicles that were wrecked and well-marked.

The military report said that "six of those killed were identified as belonging to Hamas."

It added that it would launch a criminal probe into the incident, "having found that the firing conducted during the incident raises a reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."

Which cases won't face a criminal probe?

The military said it would not investigate the airstrikes on a World Central Kitchen convoy in April 2024 that resulted in the deaths of seven of the charity's employees.

The case drew international scrutiny, with the aid group saying it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars, whose roofs bore the group’s logo visible from the air.

The military said in its report that it had mistakenly identified several individuals in the vehicles as Hamas militants and that the convoy deviated from its planned route.

It concluded that "the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."

The military also decided not to take criminal action over the killings of four staffers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate incidents in Gaza City in November 2023 and Khan Younis in February 2024.

Reactions

Rajab's grandmother, who is also named Hind Rajab, said the Israeli investigation was not enough.

"An international investigation is required to uncover the truth and hold all those responsible accountable," she said in comments to The Associated Press on Wednesday. "We call for justice, not only for Hind, but for all Gaza children."

Meanwhile, speaking to Reuters after the report's release, Red Crescent media director Eid Aziz said the deaths should never have happened in the first place.

"More important than opening the investigation is that this should have been prevented," he said. "The Palestinian Red Crescent badge is protected by international laws, and the medical staff must be protected, especially as they execute their duties and humanitarian work."

Attacks in Gaza continue despite fragile ceasefire

Meanwhile, an Israeli airstrike on a police station in Gaza City on Wednesday killed at least nine people and injured more than 20 others, according to Palestinian health authorities.

The Israeli military said the strike targeted a Hamas commander who it claimed was planning to carry out attacks against Israeli troops in Gaza.

Gaza City's Al-Shifa Hospital reported that a woman and a girl were among the dead.

Israel said it had also struck a Hamas commander in the Nuseirat area in the central Gaza Strip who had taken part in the Islamist group's attack in southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

That attack led by Hamas killed around 1,200 Israelis and prompted Israel to launch its offensive in Gaza, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, according to the territory's Health Ministry.

While fighting has largely died down since a ceasefire agareed in October last year, deadly attacks have continued and a recent US push for a long-term peace plan has stalled. 

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Could Pakistan's jailed ex-PM Imran Khan make a new deal?
entries.summary: The imprisoned former prime minister of Pakistan has been moved to a hospital for medical treatment, ushering speculation over the possibility of new political negotiations.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Could Pakistan's jailed ex-PM Imran Khan make a new deal?

August 19, 2026

The imprisoned former prime minister of Pakistan has been moved to a hospital for medical treatment, ushering speculation over the possibility of new political negotiations.

Pakistan's Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan to be shifted to a private hospital after Khan's family and political supporters repeatedly raised concerns about the 73-year-old's deteriorating health in Rawalpindi's Adiala jail.

The founder of the opposition party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has been imprisoned since August 2023 and is currently serving a 14-year sentence on corruption charges he says are politically motivated.

The former prime minister was ousted in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Khan and his supporters say Pakistan's influential military is trying to keep him out of politics, an allegation the military has denied.

Despite remaining behind bars, Khan remains politically popular. After a crackdown on the PTI following Khan's arrest, the candidates backed by him performed strongly in the February 2024 election.

"Three years in prison have not removed Khan from Pakistani politics. He remains PTI's biggest political asset, but the party's reliance on him has also exposed weaknesses in its leadership and organization," Raza Rumi, a US-based Pakistani political analyst, told DW.

Dousing speculation of new deal for Khan

The transfer of Khan to the Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical assessment has added a new dimension to the debate over his future and the possibility of political negotiations.

However, Khan's adviser Sayed Zulfi Bukhari rejected speculation that the court decision was the result of any political deal with the government.

"There is no deal between Imran Khan and anyone. This is the Supreme Court's decision, which is very much welcomed," Bukhari said.

Pakistan's Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said in a video statement on Tuesday night that the government would challenge the Supreme Court order, claiming it was unlawful.

The minister said a convicted prisoner must be treated inside the jail or at a public hospital according to law, adding that he was requesting Khan's medical tests be carried out at a government hospital instead of a private facility.

"Legally, Khan has not been granted bail nor have his convictions been suspended. He will remain a prisoner, and the hospital executive ward shall serve as a sub-jail. Unfortunately, most ordinary prisoners with far more serious ailments are never allowed such facilities by the courts," Osama Malik, a legal expert, told DW.

Pakistan's Minister of State for Interior, Talal Chaudhry, told DW that "Khan's cases will be decided by the courts."

Khan's health problems carry 'major political consequences'

PTI's Bukhari told DW that Khan "hasn't been receiving the right medical care in prison."

"That is why it has got to this stage. He has been kept in complete solitude, which has deteriorated his health," said Bukhari.

The PTI party has said Khan is suffering from various health conditions, including poor eyesight, fluctuations in blood pressure and anxiety linked to restricted contact with his family, and has been unable to access specialist medical care.

Some analysts think the health concerns are now serious enough to have prompted Supreme Court intervention.

"Beyond the medical issues, this is also about trust. The PTI and Khan's family have repeatedly questioned his access to doctors and the transparency of his treatment," said analyst Rumi.

"After three years in prison, and given his age, any deterioration in his health carries major political consequences. The state, therefore, has every reason to ensure credible and transparent medical care," he added.

The court has also ordered a medical board, including Khan's sister, Dr. Uzma Khan, and personal physician Dr. Faisal Sultan, to oversee Khan's treatment.

What future for Khan and his PTI party?

Khan's continued imprisonment has tested the PTI's ability to maintain its political strength, and the party's future will depend on whether it can maintain support without the direct political presence of its figurehead.

"Khan's political future does not look bright; he will have to compromise his political future. He will remain in jail, and even if his PTI party comes to power in the future, Khan will not be part of the government," Qamar Cheema, a political analyst, told DW.

At the same time, Khan's continued popularity makes it difficult for authorities to remove him completely from the political equation in Pakistan.

"For the state, the dilemma remains: keeping Khan imprisoned has not neutralized his influence, while releasing him without a broader settlement could revive the confrontation," said Rumi.

Rumi added that any lasting political settlement with Khan would likely require an understanding with the military establishment, which remains a key stakeholder in Pakistan.

"Such a deal could involve legal relief for Khan, greater political space for PTI, and eventually his release, in return for PTI easing its confrontation with the military and pursuing a negotiated political process. But deep mistrust remains a major obstacle, while Khan's reluctance to compromise limits the prospects for a settlement," he said.

Analyst Cheema said he doesn't think there is any possibility of a deal between the government and Khan.

"This was a genuine understanding in the Supreme Court that he should have been given proper health care," he said.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Amanal Petros: From refugee to European champion
entries.summary: Amanal Petros fled to Germany as a teenager. Now one of the world's top marathon runners, he recently won gold at the European Athletics Championships.
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Amanal Petros fled to Germany as a teenager. Now one of the world's top marathon runners, he recently won gold at the European Athletics Championships.

Amanal Petros stood in Birmingham's Victoria Square, the German flag draped over his shoulders and the gold medal resting on his chest. Eleven months after narrowly missing out on a World Championship title in Tokyo, the 31-year-old had just won his first major marathon.

After roughly 25 of the 42 kilometers, Petros picked up the pace on an incline, breaking up the lead pack. No one could keep up with him. He was able to savor the victory during the final 2 kilometers. He crossed the finish line in 2:09:11 — a record time for the men's marathon at the European Athletics Championships.

"My goal was to wrap things up early," Petros said afterwards. "That worked out perfectly."

The fact that Italian runner Pietro Riva finished just seven seconds behind him hardly reflected the commanding nature of the victory. "I had everything under control," Petros added.

Late arrival

Issues entering the United Kingdom meant Petros didn't arrive in Birmingham until Saturday — the day before the race. Media reports indicated there were difficulties with his electronic travel authorization.

"It took a very, very long time; it was awful. We were traveling back and forth for two days," he recounted. The German Athletics Association (DLV) helped resolve the issues.

The following day, a course featuring eight laps, inclines and numerous turns awaited the runners. Petros had spent months preparing for the event at altitude in Kenya.

"120 turns, the climbs. It was a huge challenge," he said after the race. Then Petros dedicated the gold medal to his mother.

"She is my queen and my source of strength," he stressed. "Thinking of her gives me new energy and motivation. She is simply the best."

His mother lives more than 5,000 kilometers (3,107 miles) away in the Tigray region of Ethiopia.

Coming to Germany alone at 16

Petros was born in the Eritrean port city of Assab in 1995. As a young child, he fled with his family — escaping the war between Eritrea and Ethiopia — to Tigray in northern Ethiopia. He grew up there with his two younger sisters. Beginning at the age of 5, he worked in the fields and tended to the animals.

Petros left Ethiopia alone at the age of 16, arriving in Germany in early 2012. He was initially housed in accommodation for asylum-seekers. His mother and sisters remained in Tigray.

In late 2021, due to the conflict in the region, Petros went more than two months without any contact with them.

"It's very hard," he told DW at the time. "Sometimes I sleep poorly and have bad dreams. But I try not to give up hope."

Running helped. "If I were to give up my sport, I would have lost everything," Petros said. "I've already lost my family, and then I would have lost the last thing I have left."

The situation in Tigray weighed on his mind even during races.

"I think about my family all the time," Petros said in 2021. While running, he tries to block out those thoughts and focus on the sport.

Talent discovered on the football pitch

Shortly after he arrived in Germany, Petros started playing football, but a club official noticed his pace and hooked him up with a local athletics club. In June 2012, just months after his arrival, Petros ran his first 10-kilometer race, winning by around two and a half minutes.

Getting acclimatized to a hew country wasn't so easy.

"Learning the language was a major challenge," Petros told DW back then. "But understanding the German mentality was an even bigger one."

He was naturalized in 2015, although at the time immigrants were usually required to wait eight years to become eligible for German citizenship. At the 2021 Olympic Games in Japan, he competed for Germany in the marathon for the first time.

In the years that followed, Petros moved closer to the international elite. In December 2025, he ran a time of 2:04:03 in Valencia, setting a new German marathon record. Another German record followed in March at the Berlin Half Marathon, where he clocked 59:22 minutes.

Near miss at Worlds

Just how close Petros had come to the world elite was evident at the World Championships in Tokyo in September 2025.

Picking up the pace with 350 meters to go, he was the first to enter the stadium and, on the home straight looked like the new world champion. But Alphonce Simbu of Tanzania passed him in the closing meters of the race. Both were clocked at 2:09:48. The photo finish decided the outcome: Petros missed gold by 0.03 seconds.

"As a professional athlete, I simply have to accept that and look ahead," Petros said afterwards. With silver, he secured Germany's first World Championship medal in the men's marathon since 1983.

"Achieving this is a huge deal for me, especially for my family, for my mom," he said after the race. He planned to send her videos of his run. "Hopefully, I'll be able to bring her to Germany for a competition someday."

Now, 11 months after that photo-finish loss in Tokyo, Petros has savored his first major international title in Birmingham.

"The race was incredibly, incredibly hard," Petros said. "But a bit of red wine will get me back on my feet quickly."

And just how much is "a bit"?

"Oh, you know, one, two, or three glasses."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Fact check: How do I spot fake social media accounts, bots and trolls?
entries.summary: If you are unsure whether to trust a message on TikTok or X, study its source. The following indicators can help you determine if you are dealing with a fake account, bot or troll.
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

If you are unsure whether to trust a message on TikTok or X, study its source. The following indicators can help you determine if you are dealing with a fake account, bot or troll.

Hundreds of thousands of inauthentic social media accounts. Tens of thousands of fake articles. Millions of automated posts.

These are some of the figures cited by the German Foreign Ministry in connection with a Russian disinformation campaign that was first detected in 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine.

Known as Doppelgänger, the operation aimed to amplify pro-Russian narratives on social media platforms in countries like Germany.

On some days, thousands of the accounts were active, posting more than once per second in a coordinated manner, the ministry said in a 2024 report. 

This campaign underscores just how important it is for users to verify the authenticity of social media accounts and identify when content is being published or amplified by bots and trolls. 

But first, what’s the difference between a bot and a troll? And how can you spot them?

DW Fact check offers tips to help you navigate today's information landscape. 

What are fake accounts?

Fake accounts are social media profiles that conceal their true identity. Some may pretend to be ordinary users; others can impersonate politicians, institutions or journalists.

Not all fake accounts have malicious intent. Some people may use pseudonyms to protect their identity or for security reasons. Activists or whistleblowers may use fake accounts to investigate sensitive issues.

What are bots?

Bots, short for robots, tirelessly comment on posts, share content, or artificially stoke online debate on marginal or otherwise overlooked topics. Sometimes, they’re entirely innocent, but sometimes they’re intent is harmful.

Good bots may automatically share news or weather forecasts, as well as earthquake alerts and satellite images on social media.

Bad bots, in contrast, are designed to imitate genuine human activity to advance a certain agenda. Depending on the algorithm, such computer programs may compose and publish social media posts or comments, follow others, or even send out friendship requests.

Bad bots can distort reality by amplifying certain political opinions on social media platforms and drawing artificial attention to certain issues.

What are trolls?

Trolls, on the other hand, are real human beings who exhibit destructive and hyperactive online behavior.

Some are even paid to harass certain public figures or media organizations as part of so-called troll factories or farms. 

One of the most prominent examples of a troll factory is the Internet Research Agency in St. Petersburg, Russia.

EUvsDisinfo, a project by the European External Action Service to counter disinformation, found that the agency had disseminated falsehoods and pro-Kremlin messages in multiple languages during various European and US election campaigns and in the lead-up to several referenda. 

How can you spot them?

Many of the fake accounts, bots and trolls may disappear before you even notice them.

At least in Europe, social media platforms are required under the Digital Services Act (DSA) to release transparency reports, including how much content they delete. 

In the last three months of 2025, for instance, Metareported taking action on 1.1 billion accounts.  

But sometimes accounts appear faster than platforms can take action. So here are some concrete tips than can help you identify them.

Identity: Check the account name, profile picture and handle

Genuine accounts tend to have a consistent digital identity. Their name, profile picture, bio and content generally tend to support the same story about who’s behind the account.

Be cautious if this does not appear to be the case. Potential red flags include:

  • A generic, stock-style or AI-generated profile picture
  • A username containing a long string of seemingly random characters and numbers
  • An account that was created recently and suddenly became very active
  • A generic bio, such as “Truth Seeker” or “Patriot”, with little or no personal information

Beyond this, verify the information through official channels.

Public figures typically have a traceable online presence. Look for links to official websites and organizations they work for. Check whether the account’s name, profile picture, personal information and handle are consistent with information published elsewhere.

Use the reverse image search method (for example on Google Lensor TinEye) to find out whether the picture used in the profile depicts someone else than claimed, or if the image has surfaced elsewhere online.  

And don’t rely on verification badges. While a blue check mark was once primarily used to confirm the identity of public figures and organizations, some platforms now allow users to buy them.

Behavior: Review what the account posts

Fake accounts, bots and troll accounts often behave differently from ordinary users.

Genuine users typically interact with others, discuss several topics and display natural patterns of activity that are often connected to their interests, profession or geographical location.

A German student posting images purporting to show an Afghan war zone? A Russian pensioner sharing photos from what she claims are Parisian anti-vaccination protests?

Neither is impossible, but both may warrant closer scrutiny. The accounts could be fake or they may be sharing disinformation. Suspicious behavior like this is typical of bots, too.

Bots also tend to post at a speed and frequency that would be nearly impossible for most people to sustain.

Trolls accounts, meanwhile, are harder to detect than downright fake accounts, as they are usually controlled by real human beings.

For trolls, it’s best to focus on the content they’re sharing. A troll’s defining feature is often their behavior rather than their identity.

Trolls are usually less interested in meaningful discussion than in provoking reactions. Their goal is frequently to increase engagement by generating outrage, sowing divisions or derailing conversations.

Network: Examine the account’s network and interactions

Fake accounts, bots and trolls rarely operate in isolation. You can find valuable clues about an account’s authenticity by examining who follows it and how other users interacts with it.

Genuine users tend to have a diverse mix of followers and interactions. By contrast, fake accounts are often part of networks that repeatedly amplify a particular narrative.

Here are some potential red flags:

  • Large numbers of followers with generic profile information
  • Comments or replies that are repetitive, identical or unrelated to the content of the post
  • Thousands of followers but little meaningful engagement
  • Followers that were created recently, have little posting history, or primarily repost content from other accounts
  • Conversations that appear one-sided, with little disagreement or diversity of opinions
  • Multiple accounts posting the same comments, links or hashtags within a short period

If you are unsure whether an account is fake, or whether content is being spread by a bot or a troll, slow down and take a closer look.

A few minutes spent examining an account’s identity, behavior and network can go a long way towards helping you distinguish genuine users from fake accounts, bots and trolls.

This article was first published in 2022 and has been revised to incorporate new developments and trends. Edited by Josh Axelrod.

This article is part of a DW Fact check series on digital literacy. Other articles include:

  • How do I spot manipulated images?
  • How do I spot AI-generated images?
  • How do I spot audio deepfakes?
  • How do I spot propaganda?

And here you can read more about how DW fact-checks fake news.
